    # System Overview and Architecture

    This chapter is for the administrator or engineer who is planning a PathScribe deployment. It says what the parts of PathScribe are, how data moves between them, what a site has to provide, and what the security controls are. It describes what the product does today. Anything that is not built is labelled Planned or Not built, and the chapter says where the nearest working feature is.

    # How to use this guide

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › How to use this guide

    Status: Built (this guide and the in-app Help button).

    The chapters follow the setup order. Chapter 2 covers Tier 1, Chapter 3 covers Tier 2, and so on to Chapter 8, which covers Tier 7. Chapter N documents Tier N-1. If you set a site up from the first chapter to the last, each screen you reach has the screens it depends on already configured. Chapter 9 holds the appendices (audit log reference and glossary).

    Every screen has a Setup sequence box. Each maintenance screen in this guide carries three lines:

    • Setup step: the screen's place in the order, for example "Tier 2, step 6". A screen that is a log, a queue or a dashboard used day to day says "Reference, not part of setup".
    • Requires: the screens that must be configured first. Each one is a link. The guide also says what happens if you skip it (an empty drop-down list, or a save that is refused).
    • Unlocks: what the screen makes possible once it is configured.

    The master Setup order page. Setup order (setup-sequence.html) lists every screen in the order you should configure it, built from those three lines. Use it as a checklist for a new site.

    The Help button. Built. A Help button sits at the top right of every Configuration screen and opens this guide at that screen's own section in a separate window that remembers its place (a new tab if the browser refuses a window), so unsaved edits are not lost. It follows the open tab and sidebar section: on the Staff tab's Role Dictionary it opens the Role Dictionary section, and on System > Departments it opens Departments. The Migration Jobs screen has one under its title. The button opens go.html#<screen id>, where <screen id> is the screen's id in this guide (for example screen-departments); go.html is produced by the guide's build and finds the right chapter page. Screens outside Configuration that have a section here (the Audit Log, Batch Management, Lockbox Drop-Off and others) are opened by an open-book button in the top bar, beside the microphone. A test fails if a Configuration tab or section has no section in this guide, so a new screen cannot ship undocumented.

    Status words. Every screen and every part of this chapter uses one of five fixed words:

    Status Meaning
    Built Works on the demonstration data and has a written service contract (docs/architecture/*_API.md) for the production server.
    Demonstration Works on the demonstration data in the browser only. The production server side is not connected yet.
    Partial Part of what the heading says is built. The section lists exactly which part.
    Planned Not built. A short paragraph says what is intended and what is known about timing.
    Not built Asked for, but no screen or contract exists. The section says so in one sentence and names the nearest thing that does exist.

    Read "Built" with care. It means the browser side works and the contract for the server is written. It does not mean the production server exists. The next part of this chapter says what the production server's state is today.

    FORMEDRIXAI INTERNAL ONLY. Some settings may be changed only by ForMedrixAI deployment or service engineers. They are the capabilities in the platform: domain, or any capability marked platformOnly, and screens shown only to such staff. In this guide their heading starts with [FORMEDRIXAI INTERNAL ONLY] and the section opens with a boxed notice that says who may change the setting and why it is restricted. The customer edition of the guide leaves those sections out. The internal edition keeps them. If you are a customer administrator and cannot see a setting that a ForMedrixAI engineer mentions, it is probably one of these.

    # Executive summary

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Executive summary

    Status: Partial. The browser application is built. The production API server, database schema and always-on services are specified in written contracts and are not built yet (see The state of the product today).

    PathScribe is an AI-assisted clinical pathology reporting and laboratory information system (LIS) from ForMedrixAI LLC. It is built for the US, the UK, the EU and other markets, and the screens are translated into six languages (English, French, German, Dutch, Korean and Spanish; the translations other than English still need review by native speakers before clinical use).

    A case runs in one of two modes, decided per case:

    • CoPilot. PathScribe is a synoptic data-capture layer on top of a host LIS. The host LIS owns the case and the final report, and PathScribe feeds structured synoptic data back to it.
    • Orchestration. PathScribe owns the case from end to end as a lightweight LIS, including AI-assisted narrative. It is used for outreach cases that have no host LIS.

    What an administrator controls is the configuration: staff and roles, the dictionaries and lookups, the workflow rules, AI behaviour, report templates, interfaces and billing rules. The chapters that follow document those screens in the order a site is set up.

    Three facts matter for planning:

    1. The production database is Microsoft SQL Server, reached through a PathScribe API server built on ASP.NET Core, with live updates over SignalR. PathScribe does not use Firebase as its production database. Some Firebase files remain in the repository from earlier work and are to be replaced.
    2. Hosting is the customer's or ForMedrixAI's choice. The design uses standard parts (containers, SQL Server, TLS certificates) and does not depend on one cloud provider. A site can use a public cloud, a private or sovereign cloud, or its own data centre.
    3. PathScribe cannot yet be deployed to production. The browser application is complete enough to demonstrate and to test against contracts. The server that would hold real patient data is not built. Plan a first deployment as a joint project with ForMedrixAI, not as an installation.

    # Architecture blueprint

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Architecture blueprint

    Status: Partial. Each part below carries its own status.

    # The parts

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Architecture blueprint › The parts
    Part What it is Status
    Browser application A React and TypeScript single-page application, served as static files. It holds no keys and, when an API server is configured, writes no patient data to browser storage. One build serves every site: each site's settings come from a config.json file beside index.html. Built
    PathScribe API server ASP.NET Core. It enforces permissions, holds the sign-in session, runs the database transactions and scheduled jobs, and calls the AI vendors, the report renderer and the interface engine. Planned. Contracts are written in docs/architecture/*_API.md. There is no server code in the repository.
    Live updates hub A SignalR hub on the API server at /hubs/live. It tells open screens that something changed, using identifiers only and never patient text. Planned. The browser side is built and tested against a test hub.
    Database Microsoft SQL Server. Planned. No schema or scripts are in the repository.
    Interface engine BridgeLink, an open-source fork of Mirth Connect (a Java server). PathScribe hands it a JSON message; the engine builds and sends the HL7 and receives replies. Partial. The message contract is written. The engine is not yet deployed or connected, and the demonstration build uses a mock engine.
    AI proxy and AI vendors The API server forwards AI requests to the configured vendor and adds the vendor key, which the browser never holds. Partial. The browser side and the per-jurisdiction vendor check are built. The server routes are Planned.
    Report renderer A service that turns a released report into a PDF, using headless Chromium driven by Playwright. Planned. Only a development stand-in exists.
    Site agent A Windows service installed at each site. It connects outward over HTTPS and prints reports and labels to network printers and writes files to Windows shares. Partial. The administration screens and the contract are built. The agent itself is Planned.
    Workstation print bridges QZ Tray or the PathScribe workstation agent, running on a bench computer to print labels to the printer beside it. QZ Tray: Built (labels print through it). Workstation agent: Built (browser side).
    Whole Slide Imaging (WSI) viewers The vendor's own viewer application (for example Leica, Roche or Hamamatsu). PathScribe tracks scan batches and opens the vendor's viewer in a new browser tab for the right slide. It never draws slide images. Built (launch link). Scan-batch status updates need the hub.

    # How data flows

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Architecture blueprint › How data flows
     Hospital or lab network                         PathScribe hosting (cloud or on-premises)
 -----------------------                         ----------------------------------------
 Bench workstation                               Static web host (browser app, config.json)
   Browser app  --- https ---------------------> PathScribe API server (ASP.NET Core)
     |   ^                                         |        |         |          |
     |   +---- wss /hubs/live (SignalR) <----------+        |         |          |
     |                                                      |         |          |
     +-- QZ Tray / workstation agent (localhost)            v         v          v
         labels to the printer beside it                SQL Server   AI proxy   Report renderer
                                                         (database)    |        (Chromium PDF)
 Site agent (Windows service) --- https, outward ------>     |         v
   report and label printers, Windows shares                 |    AI vendors (per jurisdiction policy)
                                                             |
 Interface engine (BridgeLink) <---- JSON ---- API server ---+
   HL7 to and from the host LIS, EMR, instruments
   (hosted by ForMedrixAI, or installed at the hospital)

    How to read it:

    1. Browser to API server. Every action goes through the API server with the signed-in user's identity. The browser's own permission checks only hide buttons; the server decides. The server returns fixed error codes (NOT_PERMITTED, NOT_FOUND, CONFLICT, INVALID, SIGNED_OUT, TOO_MANY_REQUESTS, TIMED_OUT, UNAVAILABLE) and never sends back text that could name a patient. Patient names and identifiers travel in a request body, never in a web address.
    2. API server to hub to browsers. After a database change commits, the server writes an event to an outbox table in the same transaction. A dispatcher then publishes it through the hub. The event carries identifiers only. A screen that receives it re-reads the data through the normal, permission-checked call. The first screens to use it are the operating-room Live Board and the Intraoperative Queue; the design target is under 500 milliseconds from commit to the second board. Without a hub, the same screens poll (every 15 seconds on the intraoperative screens).
    3. API server to AI. The browser calls /api/ai/... on its own origin. The server adds the vendor key, checks the jurisdiction's vendor and region policy, forwards the request and writes an audit record that holds no prompt text.
    4. API server to interface engine. The API server sends a JSON envelope with a transaction type (15 outbound types are listed in INTERFACE_TRANSACTIONS.md). The engine maps it to HL7 and sends it. PathScribe never builds HL7 for the wire itself. HL7 traffic stays in the engine's own message store, not on the PathScribe message bus.
    5. API server to site agent. The site agent is the only way a cloud-hosted server reaches a printer or share inside the hospital. It connects out to the server over HTTPS with a client certificate, so no inbound firewall opening is needed.
    6. Reports. The server renders every PDF that leaves PathScribe, stores one immutable, hashed document per release, and sends that same document by every channel. The browser shows a preview that is built to match what is sent.

    # Hosting and scale

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Architecture blueprint › Hosting and scale

    Status: Planned. This is the design in DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_REVIEW.md; none of it has been deployed.

    • Two supported ways to host. A public cloud, using the provider's managed database and container hosting where it fits. Or a portable package: the same containers on Kubernetes or Docker in a private cloud, a sovereign cloud or the hospital's own data centre. The package is validated once, and each hosting location then gets an installation qualification checklist.
    • Always-on parts. The API (at least one warm instance), the database (never auto-paused in production), the live-updates hub, the report renderer, and the interface engine that holds HL7 connections. Scaling to zero is not compatible with a one-second screen refresh or with STAT cases at night. Recurring jobs (retries, release timers, expiry checks) can run as short scheduled tasks.
    • Scaling the hub. Shared SaaS uses Azure SignalR Service. Private cloud and on-premises use a Redis backplane, or a single instance. Without Azure SignalR Service the load balancer needs sticky sessions and WebSockets enabled with an idle timeout above 15 seconds. The development team is still to confirm this matrix.
    • The interface engine runs either way (decided Oct 13, 2026): hosted by ForMedrixAI in the tenant's region, or installed at the hospital, from the same container image.
    • One build, many sites. npm run build:server makes the build for production. It contains no demonstration accounts or demonstration tools. Each site's addresses and sign-in settings go in its config.json (37 settings, listed in RUNTIME_SETTINGS), served with Cache-Control: no-store. PathScribe refuses to start, and names the wrong settings, if the file breaks a rule (for example an address that is not https://).
    • Browser security headers. The Content-Security-Policy, HSTS and the other headers are generated for nginx, IIS and Azure App Service, Azure Static Web Apps, Azure Front Door, or a plain list, from one definition in deploy/security-headers/. After you change an address in config.json, run the generator again so the new address is allowed.
    • Schema changes are versioned SQL scripts applied by the release pipeline, never at application start-up, and each change leaves the database usable by the previous version.

    # The state of the product today

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › The state of the product today

    Status: Demonstration for almost every data screen; see the table below for exceptions.

    Read this part before you promise a customer a go-live date. It was checked against the repository on Oct 21, 2026.

    What runs today. The browser application runs on browser-held demonstration services. About 170 service folders in src/services/ follow one pattern: an interface, a demonstration version that keeps its data in the browser, and (for nearly all of them) a server version that calls the API. The application picks the server version when VITE_API_BASE_URL is set in config.json, and the demonstration version otherwise. When an API server is configured, demonstration data is kept in memory and not written to browser storage.

    What is connected to a production API. None. The server versions exist in the browser code and have fake-server tests that check every route, but the API server that would answer them is not in the repository and has not been built (the work is assigned to the India team, from the contracts). Nothing has been tried against a real server. Server-side versions in the browser code are written for all but three services:

    Service with no server version yet Why
    Action registry (voice and hotkey matching) Synchronous and in memory. Only its saved settings would go to the server, through the configuration service.
    AI instruction service Its rules run in the browser over injected storage; storage goes through the configuration and audit services.
    Interface dictionary service Same: rules run in the browser. Storage goes through the configuration and audit services.

    Live updates already use SignalR in the browser (signalRLiveUpdateService.ts), but the hub is not built.

    What blocks a production deployment (from the readiness review, status at Batch 641):

    Blocker State
    API server and SQL Server schema Open. Not started.
    Blob storage for report PDFs, exports and held releases Contract written. Storage and endpoints open.
    Server-side scheduled jobs (about ten timers) Open. Until each job moves, the browser runs it while someone is signed in. VITE_SERVER_JOBS hands a job to the server by name.
    Report renderer service Cytology template done. The hosted service is open.
    Sign-in through the server (backend-for-frontend), runtime identity-provider configuration Runtime configuration done. The server part is open.
    Interface engine, always-on, with the edge rules Contract written. Hosting and endpoints open.
    Site agent Contract and screens done. The agent is open.
    Hub and push updates Browser side done. The hub is open.
    Retire the earlier Vercel api/ functions, Firebase services and functions/ Open. Three screens (Engraver Monitor, QA deficiency list, material tracking history) still read Firebase-backed services.

    Other open items an administrator should know about:

    • The browser enforces permissions today, and the server enforcement is not built. The capability checks run in the browser's services. A server must repeat every check before real patient data is held. See Security model.
    • Screen-reader testing by a person has not been done. Automated accessibility checks (WCAG 2.1 A and AA rules, in Chromium) pass, but a person has not yet tested with NVDA or VoiceOver (PS-687).
    • Firefox has not been run through the automated suite in the build workspace. A hand check in Chrome, Edge and Firefox is open (PS-718).
    • Translations in French, German, Dutch, Korean and Spanish need native-speaker review before clinical use.
    • The continuous-integration pipeline is written but runs only once the repository is on GitHub (planned for the end of October 2026).

    # Database

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › System prerequisites › Database

    Status: Planned. No schema, scripts or database code are in the repository.

    • Engine. Microsoft SQL Server. The same engine runs as Azure SQL Database (serverless or provisioned), SQL Server on a virtual machine, SQL Server in Linux containers (official Microsoft images for 2017 to 2025; x86-64 Linux hosts only; a licence is required), or AWS RDS for SQL Server.
    • Never auto-pause a production database. A paused database turns the first screen of the morning, or a STAT case at night, into a failed request. Auto-pause is acceptable for test and training tenants only. On Azure SQL serverless it is turned off with -1.
    • Starting point for size. The readiness review recommends a minimum of 2 virtual cores for a production tenant "until load testing says otherwise". It is a recommendation, not a tested requirement. Storage, memory, IOPS and growth per case: Not yet specified.
    • Schema changes. Versioned scripts applied by the release pipeline before the API container starts, never at application start-up.
    • Backups. Point-in-time restore is the design for the audit tables. Backup schedule, retention, recovery time objective and recovery point objective: Not yet specified.
    • AWS note. AWS has no serverless SQL Server, and a changed instance class means downtime (shortened by Multi-AZ). Licence cost applies.
    • Blob storage for report PDFs, exports and held releases: Azure Blob or an S3-compatible store, per tenant, private, encrypted at rest and in the tenant's hosting region (contract: BLOB_STORAGE_API.md). PathScribe stores no images or attachments, only links to the lab's imaging system.

    # Network

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › System prerequisites › Network
    Need Detail
    TLS everywhere Every server address in config.json must be https://. Plain http:// is allowed only to the same computer in a development build, or for an internal deployment that sets "https": false in its security-headers origins file (which then drops HSTS).
    Browser to API and hub HTTPS to the API server. WebSockets (wss://) to /hubs/live. Leave Server-Sent Events and long polling enabled as fallbacks, because some hospital proxies block WebSockets. Load balancers need WebSockets enabled and an idle timeout above 15 seconds.
    Allowed addresses config.json addresses (API, identity providers, hub, renderer, interface receiver, AI and terminology endpoints, error monitoring) become the browser's Content-Security-Policy. Re-run the headers generator after any change.
    Identity provider Reachable from the browser (and from the server, once the server holds the sign-in). Redirect addresses for Microsoft Entra ID: https://<pathscribe host>/auth/callback/microsoft and https://<pathscribe host>/auth/signing/microsoft.
    Site agent Outbound HTTPS (port 443) only, on its own host name (for example agent.<tenant domain>) that demands a client certificate. No inbound firewall opening. A TLS-inspecting proxy must pass that host through untouched, because inspection breaks the client certificate.
    Site agent reach (set locally by hospital IT) The printer subnets, the printer ports (default 9100, 515, 631 and 443), the UNC roots for shares, and the hosts documents may be downloaded from. PathScribe cannot change this list.
    HL7 link Orders in and results out use the interface engine. The link is secured with a site-to-site VPN or MLLP over TLS. A message is acknowledged only once it is stored durably.
    Fixed outbound address SFTP file drops need a fixed outbound IP address for the hospital's allow-list (a NAT gateway or firewall egress), and a pinned host key.
    E-fax and email An SMTP gateway on port 587 with authentication.
    Bandwidth and latency Not yet specified. The design target for a general screen refresh is 800 ms at the 95th percentile from commit to render; for the operating-room boards, under 500 ms. The first page load is 0.70 MB compressed (target 1 MB).
    Hosting region One region is chosen per deployment. The API server's /api/config can report the database and blob regions, which the AI Behavior tab shows (see AI Behavior). That endpoint is Planned.

    # Client workstation

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › System prerequisites › Client workstation

    Status: Built, with open checks noted.

    • Supported browsers (decided Oct 15, 2026): current Chrome, Microsoft Edge and Firefox. Safari is not supported. The automated tests run in Chromium (the engine of Chrome and Edge). Firefox is run only on request, has not yet been run in the build workspace, and a hand check in all three is open (PS-718). In Chrome and Edge drop-down lists are drawn as styled panels; Firefox shows its own list. Behaviour is the same.
    • Browser features used. WebAssembly (the spell checker), Web Workers, and (when the person grants them) camera, microphone and screen capture, for grossing photographs, dictation and enhancement-request screenshots. The Permissions-Policy header allows these for PathScribe only.
    • Label printing from a bench computer. QZ Tray (Built) or the PathScribe workstation agent (Built, browser side) must run on the computer. They listen only on the computer itself: the workstation agent on wss://127.0.0.1 ports 9100 to 9102, and QZ Tray on localhost ports 8181, 8282, 8383 and 8484. If the page cannot reach QZ Tray, the label opens in the browser's print window and a message says the label printer is not connected.
    • Allow local-network access. Chrome and Edge ask the person's permission for local addresses. Hospital IT can pre-approve PathScribe with the LocalNetworkAccessAllowedForUrls policy.
    • QZ Tray prompts. QZ Tray asks "Allow this website to use your printers?" until print requests are signed with the customer's certificate. Signing is Planned (it needs the API server). Until then the person may be asked once per workstation. The decision (Oct 16, 2026) is one self-signed certificate per customer, which has an expiry date that IT must renew and redeploy; see docs/product/QZ_TRAY_CERTIFICATE_GUIDE.md. The steps for each device-management tool are marked "Test first" because they have not been run on a pilot machine.
    • Label printers. Thermal printers that take ZPL. Report printers on the network are reached through the site agent. Network report printing does not work from the browser today.
    • Screen readers. Automated accessibility checks pass; testing by a person with NVDA or VoiceOver is open (PS-687).
    • Languages. English, French, German, Dutch, Korean and Spanish, plus Belgian Dutch and Belgian French wording.
    • Monitor size, minimum processor and memory: Not yet specified.
    • Whole Slide Imaging viewers. The vendor's viewer must be installed or reachable from the workstation as that vendor requires. PathScribe only opens the viewer in a new tab, using a launch address template you enter once for each viewer, with the slide's barcode filled in. It is configured in Vendor Integrations. PathScribe ships no viewer address.

    # Security model

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model

    Status: Partial. Nearly every control below is built in the browser and has a written server contract. The server that must repeat each check is not built (see The state of the product today). A browser check is a courtesy; the server's check is the control. Do not describe any control here as protecting real patient data until the server side exists.

    This part says what each control does. It does not say that using it makes a laboratory compliant with any law or standard. The laboratory's own policies, contracts and quality system decide that.

    # Single sign-on

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model › Single sign-on

    Status: Partial. OpenID Connect (OIDC): browser side Built. Server side Planned.

    • Protocol. OpenID Connect, authorization code flow with PKCE, with the app registered as a public single-page-application client (no client secret). It is generic, so it works with Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Ping and Keycloak. Microsoft Entra ID is the first target. The Entra authority must name a tenant: /common, /organizations and /consumers are refused because they would let any Microsoft account in.
    • Google sign-in is not offered, because Google's token endpoint demands a client secret. A hospital on Google Workspace can federate Google through Entra ID or Okta.
    • Nobody is created by signing in. Only staff who are already provisioned and active can sign in. The identity is matched to a staff record by the provider's permanent subject (Entra's oid, otherwise sub), never by email alone. The first sign-in may link by email if the email is trusted (verified, or a tenant-specific Entra authority); a setting can turn that off so an administrator links each account. Refusals (not provisioned, inactive, ambiguous, already linked, no application access) are shown with a plain message and audited. See Members.
    • Demonstration builds also offer password sign-in. A production build (VITE_AUTH_MODE set to sso) has no demonstration accounts in it.
    • Tokens. Today the browser holds the tokens in sessionStorage (this tab only, gone when the tab closes). Planned for production (decided Oct 3 and Oct 15, 2026): the API server holds the tokens and the browser gets only an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite session cookie with an anti-forgery header. The browser never carries a JWT, and the hub uses the same cookie. This needs shared session storage (SQL Server or Redis) on the server.
    • Registering the app in Entra ID (steps for hospital IT, from AUTHENTICATION_OIDC.md): a single-tenant registration with platform Single-page application and the two redirect addresses listed under Network, no client secret, the optional email claim in the ID token, and an exposed API scope granted to the application.
    • Accounts and roles from the directory. Automatic account sync (SCIM: joiners, changes and leavers) is Planned for the server phase. Mapping directory groups to PathScribe roles is Planned for after the first release. When it comes, a group may grant only bench roles, never Admin, Lab Director, Template Approver or anything with signing authority, and each mapping needs a second administrator's approval. Today roles are assigned by hand in Members and Roles.

    # SAML 2.0

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model › Single sign-on › SAML 2.0

    Status: Not built.

    PathScribe has no SAML 2.0 sign-in, no SAML library and no SAML screen. A search of the whole repository finds the word only in two design documents. The nearest thing that works is OIDC, above. The documented direction for shared SaaS hosting is that hospitals sign in through a PathScribe identity broker (Microsoft Entra ID External ID), which speaks SAML or OIDC to the hospital's directory and plain OIDC to PathScribe, so "PathScribe never handles SAML". That broker is Planned and not built. A private-cloud or dedicated deployment connects straight to the hospital's own Entra ID by OIDC. A hospital that can only offer SAML today should say so to ForMedrixAI during planning, or federate SAML into Entra ID or Okta, which then speak OIDC to PathScribe.

    # Role-based access control

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model › Role-based access control

    Status: Demonstration. The checks run in the browser's services. The server-side enforcement (AUTHORIZATION_API.md, phase 4) is Planned.

    • Capabilities. Everything PathScribe enforces is a named capability in the form domain:object:verb, for example config:retention-policy:manage. The catalog (capabilityCatalog.ts) is the only list and holds about 320 capabilities (322 at the time of writing; the number grows with releases). A capability is added only together with its check, and a test fails the build if a capability has no check. Each capability has a risk level. For a high-risk capability, every check at an action is written to the audit log, allowed or refused, and every export is high risk.
    • Roles. A role is a set of capabilities. A staff member holds one or more roles and a facility assignment (an empty assignment means all facilities). Scope belongs to the assignment, not the role. A check passes only when a held role grants the capability, every capability it requires is also granted, and the action is within the person's facilities. A refusal gives a reason (not granted, requirement not granted, out of scope, facility unknown).
    • Built-in roles. Sixteen: Pathologist, Resident, Fellow, Pathologist's Assistant, Admin, Physician, OR Staff, Template Author, Template Approver, Lab Director, QA Reviewer, Accessioner, Histotechnologist, Cytotechnologist, Molecular Technologist and Superadmin. Physician and OR Staff are directory entries with no application access. Seeds follow least privilege: a Pathologist holds no configuration capabilities by default. An administrator can change roles and add roles in Roles, except Superadmin.
    • No bypass for any role. Superadmin is a role granted capabilities like any other, and the check has no shortcut for it. Admin does not imply anything either. Superadmin holds every capability except config:ai-prompt:approve (approving the AI instructions): that is withheld for separation of duties, so only the laboratory (the Lab Director) approves what its own AI is told, and ForMedrixAI support never does.
    • Superadmin is reserved for ForMedrixAI support. It is held only through a support sign-in. A hospital cannot assign it, edit it or see it in the staff role picker, and a staff record that names it gets nothing from it. The server-side source of that identity (ForMedrixAI's own identity tenant) is Planned.
    • Platform-only capabilities. Six capabilities in the platform: domain count only from Superadmin (cross-tenant case viewing, governing bodies, signing rules, and the interface dictionary's manage, publish and simulate). A hospital role cannot hold them. Their screens are marked [FORMEDRIXAI INTERNAL ONLY] in this guide.
    • Tenant boundary. Every user and case carries an organisationId. Cross-tenant reach is limited to support access (below). Enforcement today is in the browser; a server-side query layer that enforces it is Planned.
    • Case privacy. A person who cannot open a case gets the same neutral message as for a case that does not exist. A typed or pasted accession number proves nothing, and a message turns a number into a link only if the reader can open that case. The server must give the same answer (for example 404) for "no such case" and "you may not see it", with no difference in body, headers or timing.
    • Screens. Each screen has its own screen:<name>:open capability. Home and the hubs show only the tiles the person may open, and the route checks again.
    • Voice and keyboard commands are not access control and are never used to grant access.
    • Where to administer it. Roles, Members and the Staff tab. Role and capability changes are audited.

    # Multi-factor authentication and sign-out re-authentication

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model › Multi-factor authentication and sign-out re-authentication

    Status: Partial. Browser side Built. The authenticator for demonstration accounts is Simulated. Server side Planned.

    • Single sign-on users. The identity provider asks for the second factor. PathScribe reads the ID token and accepts MFA when amr contains mfa, or names methods from two different families (knowledge, possession, inherence), or acr names a multi-factor class. A password alone is not MFA. If the organisation requires MFA and the token does not say so, the sign-in is refused with a plain message. The provider must be set to send these claims (Entra: a Conditional Access policy that requires MFA; Okta: an authentication policy with a possession factor; Keycloak: map the authentication level to acr and add an amr mapper).
    • Policy per organisation. In Session Security: who is asked (no one, the roles that sign reports, or everyone; default no one), how many minutes before a signature needs a fresh code (1 to 720, default 30), and how many hours before the second factor expires and the session ends (1 to 72, default 12). Saved with config:session-security:manage and audited.
    • Step up at a signature. When the last second factor is older than the step-up time, signing asks again: a fresh code for password sessions, or a fresh sign-in at the provider (prompt=login) whose token must again assert MFA.
    • Demonstration accounts. A Simulated time-based authenticator (RFC 6238) with recovery codes shown once. It is in the demonstration build only. A server build has no simulated factor, so a person who is not using single sign-on and is asked for MFA is told it is unavailable and cannot sign in. Reset of an enrolment needs auth:mfa-enrolment:reset.
    • Lockout. Five failed codes lock the check for 15 minutes. Five failed password sign-ins lock an email for 15 minutes. These counts are kept in the browser today; the server must keep them. With single sign-on the provider applies its own lockout.
    • Sign-out authentication policy (Built, Demonstration). Per performing facility: a password at every sign-out (the default, strict) or once per session (session, with a length of 15, 30, 60 or 240 minutes), with an optional second factor. A session ends on timeout, sign-out or a change of role. The screen warns that the once-per-session mode departs from what 21 CFR Part 11 (11.200(a)(1)) expects for later signings, so the customer's quality system decides.
    • Biometric signing (WebAuthn, Touch ID or Windows Hello) is an optional confirmation. Each person enrols their own device and the password always works as well. The server version of the biometric calls is written but the screens do not yet use it.
    • Not built: remote sign-out restriction by network, workstation-lock expiry of a sign-out session, SMS and hardware-key second factors, a server-side policy store.
    • Where to administer it. Session Security.

    # Session security

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model › Session security

    Status: Partial. Idle time-out Built (browser). Server-held session Planned.

    • Idle time-out. An organisation-wide default in Session Security, chosen from 5, 10, 15, 20, 30 or 60 minutes. The default is 15. A performing laboratory can set its own value in the Facility Dictionary. When a case is open the laboratory's value applies; elsewhere (Home, Worklist) the organisation value applies. On time-out the person is signed out, and unsaved drafts are kept, not discarded.
    • Same account, second tab. Signing in again as the same user in another tab supersedes the earlier session in the same browser, with a prompt.
    • Server rule. The server also ends a session whose token has expired, so a closed or frozen browser cannot keep one open.
    • Browser storage. With an API server configured, no patient data is written to browser storage. Only display preferences, workstation settings (scan station, display profile, window positions) and the sign-in session touch it.
    • Transport and page protection. The generated headers set a strict Content-Security-Policy (no inline script, no eval, no framing), HSTS on https deployments, nosniff, a no-referrer policy (addresses can carry case ids) and a restricted Permissions-Policy. Report HTML is sanitised before it is shown. The browser holds no AI, terminology or vendor key, and a test fails the build if one appears in the front end.
    • Error reports. Crash reports can go to Sentry or a hospital's own collector, off by default. A report holds only an error name, a scrubbed message (no quoted text, email addresses or runs of three or more digits), at most ten stack frames, the route with numeric segments replaced, and a reference. It needs two settings in config.json and, for a US customer, a signed Business Associate Agreement with the provider, or for the EU and UK a data-processing agreement and EU data residency. Self-hosting avoids both.
    • Where to administer it. Session Security and Facility Dictionary.

    # Support access

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model › Support access

    Status: Partial. Browser side Built. Server side Planned.

    The hospital, as data controller, decides whether ForMedrixAI support may reach its data. "Support access" means a Superadmin session reaching an organisation the person is not a staff member of.

    • Policy per organisation. Disabled (support gets nothing, including Superadmin), Approval required (the default), or Always allowed. Under Approval required, support asks per ticket with a reason of at least 10 characters. An approver in the hospital (not the requester) approves or rejects. An approval lasts the organisation's access window (30 minutes, 1, 2, 4 or 8 hours; the default is 2) or less if support ends it or the hospital revokes it.
    • The hospital's own audit stream. Separate from the main audit log: requests, decisions, expiries, refused opens, case opens and edits, every list or search that disclosed cases (case ids; search criteria names, never values), policy changes and exports. Each entry is hash-chained to the one before it, so a changed or removed entry breaks the chain, and the screen shows the tamper check. Export is CSV or JSON.
    • Capabilities. config:support-access:policy, config:support-access:approve and config:support-audit:view, seeded to Admin. Opening another organisation's case also needs platform:cross-tenant-cases:view, which only Superadmin can hold, and is audited.
    • Not built (server work): the originating IP address and country (the browser records them empty), email and webhook notification to approvers (today an in-app message), ending access when the ticket closes, PDF export of the stream (CSV and JSON exist; a PDF function is written in the browser), the stream in its own append-only per-tenant table, and support session tokens bound to the ticket and expiry.
    • Where to administer it. Support Access.

    # Audit logging

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model › Audit logging

    Status: Partial. Browser side Built. Server storage Planned.

    • What is recorded. User actions, sign-outs, amendments, voice events, system events and AI calls. Every high-risk capability check is recorded whether allowed or refused. Configuration changes by an authorised person are audited. Some record the old and new values (for example the AI vendor policy and signing-authority overrides); for many settings the log holds only the entry that the capability check was allowed, not the new value. See System Logs for what each entry holds.
    • No patient data in the detail. Audit detail text is literal English and is built to hold no patient names, dates of birth, MRNs or clinical values. It uses identifiers and configuration names. Passwords, codes and secrets are never recorded.
    • Server design. Append-only tables (insert and select permissions only), each audit row written in the same transaction as the change it records, a hash-chained stream for support access, and point-in-time backups. Exported audit archives on immutable storage are a per-hospital option. Planned: none of it exists until the server is built. The browser version keeps the log in demonstration storage.
    • Retention. See Data retention.
    • Where to read it. System Logs, with the interface and financial views System Logs: interfaces and System Logs: financial.

    # Redaction of patient data in support screenshots

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model › Redaction of patient data in support screenshots

    Status: Built.

    When a user sends an Enhancement Request, the app takes a screenshot and covers every element tagged as patient data before the image leaves the browser. Anything that shows a patient name, date of birth, MRN or national identifier, accession or case number, or patient contact or insurance detail is tagged data-phi with its kind. Toasts that name a case are wrapped so they are covered too. Staff names are not treated as patient data. A test reads every source file and fails the build on an untagged place, with no exception list. Limits to plan around: free text that happens to contain an identifier (audit detail, interface exception reasons) cannot be recognised by any code check, so those cells are covered as a whole; and the check reads names, not types, so a value passed through a generic list can be missed (one such case was found and fixed in Batch 368, and twenty screens were then checked in a browser).

    # AI vendor policy and hosting regions

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model › AI vendor policy and hosting regions

    Status: Partial. Browser check Built. Server proxy check Planned.

    • Why. Some jurisdictions name which AI vendors are allowed or forbidden. PathScribe is vendor-neutral and checks every AI call before sending it.
    • The rule. For each jurisdiction, and optionally each facility: the AI services allowed, and the hosting regions allowed for each service. No rule means every service is allowed. A facility rule narrows its jurisdiction's rule, and the call must pass both. Where a rule limits regions, a call whose region is not recorded is refused. The services are named by request shape: structured messages (Anthropic), chat completions (OpenAI), chat completions managed (Azure OpenAI), model gateway (AWS Bedrock), structured content (Google Gemini) and custom (a self-hosted model). The configured hosting region is saved with the AI provider setting.
    • When refused. The feature carries on without AI and says "AI is not available for this jurisdiction" where it can. The call is never sent to a different vendor instead.
    • The server must repeat the check. A browser check can be bypassed, so the server's AI proxy must make the same check on every route and is the one that counts. It must choose the service and region from the saved setting, never from the request body, answer 403 with code AI_VENDOR_NOT_ALLOWED, and audit the refusal. Planned.
    • Keys. The browser never holds an AI vendor key. In production the keys live in the server's secret store (for example Azure Key Vault). The saved setting holds the provider, model, endpoint and deployment name, never a key.
    • What the server should also do (Planned): audit each AI call (who, case, facility and jurisdiction checked, service, model, hosting region, feature, tokens, outcome; never the prompt, which can hold patient data), rate-limit per user and organisation, and check that a Business Associate Agreement or data-processing agreement is in place for the chosen provider.
    • Disclosed gap. In the browser, a provider setting of mock sends AI requests to the Anthropic route through the proxy, so a demonstration site set to mock still calls the proxy. A jurisdiction that does not allow Anthropic refuses it.
    • Human review. AI output is a suggestion. The screens that use it show it for the clinician to accept or reject; see the AI chapter (Chapter 5).
    • Where to administer it. The AI vendor policy card and the hosting-regions card on the AI Behavior tab. Changing a rule needs config:ai-vendor-policy:manage (Admin and Lab Director by default), and each change is audited as AI_VENDOR_POLICY_CHANGED.

    # Data retention

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model › Data retention

    Status: Partial. The settings are Built. Nothing purges data by them yet; the purge job is server work.

    Data Retention holds four periods: AI suggestions (default 90 days), audit logs (default 365 days), case snapshots (default 7 years) and the report archive (default 10 years). The screen warns that the minimum audit-log retention is 90 days and that reductions below regulatory minimums need sign-off from the institution's compliance officer. Saving needs config:retention-policy:manage. Retention of physical specimens and blocks is handled by the disposal queue and case-level Retention Holds, which follow the jurisdiction (RCPath for the UK, CAP and CLIA for the US). Immutable report documents in blob storage are their own protection against deletion. Retention periods for backups: Not yet specified.

    # HIPAA and CLIA: the controls the product has

    Home › Administrator Guide › System Overview and Architecture › Security model › HIPAA and CLIA: the controls the product has

    Status: Partial. The table lists controls that exist in the browser build. No control protects real patient data until the server side exists, and using these controls does not make a laboratory compliant with HIPAA, CLIA or any other law. Compliance depends on the laboratory's policies, contracts, hosting and quality system.

    Area What PathScribe has Status Where

    Access control (least privilege) Capabilities and roles, facility scope, no bypass for any role, case privacy Demonstration Roles
    Automatic logoff Idle time-out (organisation default, per-laboratory override); drafts are kept Built (browser) Session Security
    Person authentication Single sign-on, provider MFA checked from the token, step-up at a signature, optional device check Partial Session Security
    Audit controls Audit log of actions, high-risk checks, configuration changes; hash-chained support stream Partial System Logs
    Transmission security https required for every server address, HSTS, strict content policy; mutual TLS for the site agent Built (browser and headers). Server Planned Network
    Vendor access Hospital-controlled, ticket-linked, time-limited support access with its own audit Partial Support Access
    Minimum necessary in tools Patient data redacted from support screenshots; no patient text in web addresses, errors or hub messages; crash reports scrubbed Built Redaction
    Third parties handling patient data AI vendor policy per jurisdiction, region limits, keys held by the server; Business Associate Agreement or data-processing agreement needed for each provider Partial AI Behavior
    Report integrity One immutable, hashed (SHA-256) report document per release, sent unchanged by every channel; versioned case saves with conflict detection Built (contract); server Planned Chapter 6
    Data retention Configurable periods; disposal queue and Retention Holds for specimens Partial Data Retention
    CLIA: signing authority Participation types and per-country signing rules decide who may sign, with audited local overrides Built Participation Types, Country Signing Rules
    CLIA: cytology workload and competency A daily workload limit for GYN cytology screening, with staff and facility overrides, and routing of a new cytotechnologist's sign-outs to a supervisor for countersign until competency assessments are documented Built (browser). The server records screening time with its own clock; Planned Daily Workload Cap, Country and laboratory rules
    Facility identity on reports A facility record holds its CLIA or ISO 15189 number, shown in report headers Built Facility Dictionary

    Not built or not specified: encryption at rest for the SQL Server database (no setting or requirement is written in the repository; the blob containers are specified as encrypted at rest); a backup and disaster-recovery specification; a server-side tamper-evident audit store; independent penetration test or security certification (none is recorded in the repository); and any statement of compliance.

    # Tier 1: Primary System Prerequisites (Configure First)

    Tier 1 is the part of Configuration that every other setting stands on. It answers four questions before anything else can be set up: which laboratory sites exist, who may do what, which physical devices the sites use, and which organisation-wide rules apply. Later tiers read from it. A department asks for a facility. A report template routes by role. A label prints through a printer profile. If a Tier 1 screen is empty, the screens that depend on it show empty pickers or refuse to save.

    Configure Tier 1 in this order. Each screen below carries a Setup sequence box with the same information, and the builder checks that no screen requires one that comes after it.

    1. Facility Dictionary: the organisation, its performing laboratories and ordering clients.
    2. Participation Types: the case roles (primary, resident, consultant) and who may sign out.
    3. Roles: what each job may open and change.
    4. Delegation Types: the ways a case or report can be handed over.
    5. Members: the people.
    6. Credentialing: supervised-practice reviews for new staff.
    7. Session Security: idle sign-out, second factor and sign-out policy.
    8. Support Access: whether ForMedrixAI support may reach your data.
    9. Equipment: the register of every device.
    10. Printer Profiles: what each label printer can do and how a browser reaches it.
    11. Site agents: the program that prints and moves files on a site's network.
    12. Scan Stations: the benches a terminal can identify itself as.
    13. Print Settings: label sizes, barcode rules and print behaviour.
    14. Label Designer: the layout of each label.
    15. Workstations: registered computers with a token.
    16. Workstation Groups: benches grouped by discipline and area.
    17. Grossing Hardware: cameras and scales at the grossing benches.
    18. Data Retention: how long records are kept.
    19. Case Mask Configuration: accession numbering.
    20. Field Requirements: which fields a page needs before it can be saved.
    21. External Resources: reference links.

    Five screens are references, not setup steps: the System tab, the Staff tab, the Scope reference, the Jurisdiction overview and the Simulated print log.

    Status words. Each screen shows one of the five status words defined in the authoring standard: Built, Demonstration, Partial, Planned, Not built. Today most data services run on the browser's demo data, and the production API is connected service by service. Where a screen already has a production service and a contract in docs/architecture, it is Built. Where the screen works only in the browser, or its effect is not applied anywhere yet, it is Demonstration.

    # Part A: Enterprise and Facilities Management

    Home › Configuration › System

    This part holds the System tab that contains every screen in Parts A, C and D, and the one screen that defines your organisation's structure.

    How the hierarchy works. There is no separate "Enterprise" screen and no "hospital" or "clinic" type. Everything is a facility on the Facility Dictionary. A facility marked as an Enterprise is the top level (your organisation). Other facilities point to it as their Parent Enterprise, and are the affiliates. What a facility does is set by its roles (Performing Lab, Ordering Facility and so on), not by a type. Locations (ward, room, bed) hang under one facility. The Scope reference lists which settings are set once for the enterprise and which are set per facility.

    Where date, time, timezone and language are set. There is no single "global date and time" screen. Each is set in a different place:

    What Where it is set Scope
    Time zone One Facility Timezone choice on the Contribution Dashboard settings screen. It decides which day or month a signed-out case is counted in, and the year used by accession numbering. Whole organisation. Default America/Phoenix.
    Date and number format Follows the display language chosen in the top bar. The Identifier Formats tab of the facility editor shows the jurisdiction's date format, time format and locale read-only. Each user's browser.
    Display language The language button in the top bar. Choices: English, French, French (Belgium), German, Dutch, Dutch (Belgium), Korean, Spanish. Stored in the browser as pathscribe_language. Each user, each browser.
    Report language Report language on the facility's General tab. Each performing lab.
    Spelling language Spelling language on the staff member's record. Each person.
    Site agent update window Times in the site's local time on the Site agents screen. Each site.

    Stored times are always UTC. Nothing in Tier 1 changes that.

    # Facility Dictionary

    Home › Configuration › System › Integrations › Facility Configuration

    Status: Built

    1. Navigation: Configuration tab System > group Integrations > Facility Configuration. The page heading reads "Facility Configuration". It is the same screen that Chapter 3 lists as Facility Configuration. 2. Maintenance item: Facility Dictionary

    3. Business purpose and scope. A facility is any site or organisation PathScribe knows about: your own laboratories, the clinics and hospitals that send you specimens, and the reference laboratories you send work to. Each facility carries its roles, contact details, the codes that match inbound orders to it, its turnaround targets, report delivery choices and print routing. The top-level organisation is a facility with Enterprise ticked. Almost every other screen asks for a facility, so this is the first screen to fill.

    4. Prerequisites and dependencies. Nothing comes before it. The Place of Service Code list on the General tab reads the code dictionary, and the Model list on the AI & Performance tab lists only models with a passing validation study. Both are optional. Skip the facility and every other screen's facility picker is empty.

    How spell check uses this list. The checker tries a word against, in order: the person's own dictionary, this facility word list (the list of the case's performing laboratory), the regional spelling rule, PathScribe's pathology word list, and the language's standard dictionary. The first list that accepts the word wins. Words with digits, capital-letter abbreviations of up to six letters, and web or e-mail addresses are never checked. The language comes from the case, then the pathologist's Spelling language on the Staff record, then the facility's jurisdiction, then US English. Each addition or removal here is recorded in the audit log under "Facility spelling dictionary word added" or "removed". Only single words can be added. The pathology word lists for French, German, Dutch, Spanish and Korean are starter lists that still need native-speaker review, so expect some correct specialist terms to be underlined until you add them here.

Secure messaging tab: config:secure-messaging:manage. Admin and Lab Director hold these by default. Field-level changes the page audits are listed above. Known limits. Sending by secure messaging is simulated: messageService.sendSecureEmail records the message but no real gateway transport exists yet (PS-332). The AI & Performance tab text points the release buffer default at "Configuration > System > LIS Integration", but that default lives on Post-Sign-Out Release Buffer.

    # Part B: User Management, Roles and the Permission Matrix

    Home › Configuration › Staff

    This part covers who can sign in and what each person may do. Access in PathScribe is built from capabilities. A capability is one permission written as domain:object:verb, for example config:roles:manage. A role is a named bundle of capabilities. A person gets capabilities through their roles, limited to the facilities on their record. Capabilities marked high risk are written to the audit log when they are used.

    The permission matrix. The matrix is the capability list on the Roles screen: every capability, grouped, with a check for each role. The catalog and the starting assignments are fixed in the product (capabilityCatalog.ts and capabilitySeeds.ts). Four rules matter when you plan roles:

    • Built-in roles. Pathologist, Resident, Fellow, PA, Admin, Physician, OR Staff, Template Author, Template Approver, Lab Director, QA Reviewer, Superadmin, Accessioner, Histotechnologist, Cytotechnologist and Molecular Technologist ship ready-made. A role you add yourself starts with no configuration capabilities.
    • Admin and Lab Director. Admin holds every configuration capability. Lab Director holds the same set except two groups: the administration group (config:roles:manage, config:staff:edit, config:staff-access:assign, config:staff-password:manage, config:field-requirements:manage, auth:mfa-enrolment:reset, config:demo-data:reset) and drafting protocols. So only Admin and Superadmin manage roles, staff and field requirements.
    • Superadmin. A ForMedrixAI role. It holds every capability except config:ai-prompt:approve, a hospital cannot change it, and a hospital cannot assign it to its own staff.
    • Separation of duties. config:clinical-mismatch-rules:manage and config:ai-prompt:approve cannot be held together by one role or one person. The save is refused.

    A refused configuration change shows the reason CONFIG_NOT_PERMITTED. A section you cannot change opens read-only.

    # Part C: Workstation, Printer, Label Generator and Scanner Mappings

    Home › Configuration › System › Workstation & Hardware

    This part covers the physical side: the register of devices, the printers and the program that drives them, the benches that scan and print, and the rules for labels. Most of these screens are in the Workstation & Hardware group, which shows a shared Facility selector above the sidebar. Choose a site there once and Print Settings, Printer Profiles, Scan Stations, Site agents, Equipment and Grossing Hardware all show that site. Workstation Groups is in the Lab Materials & Workflows group.

    Suggested order. Register the devices first (Equipment), then say what each printer can do (Printer Profiles), then install and configure the site agent, then name the benches (Scan Stations), then set the print rules and the label layouts, then register computers and group the benches.

    What a label needs. A printed label goes through four things. Print Settings picks the label size, barcode type and printer profile. Label Designer lays out the fields. Printer Profiles says how a browser reaches the printer. The Facility editor's Printing tab and the site agent say where reports and labels go on the site's network. With no API server, nothing reaches a real printer: each print is recorded on the Simulated print log.

    # Case Mask Configuration

    Home › Configuration › System › Integrations › Case Mask Configuration

    Status: Built

    1. Navigation: Configuration tab System > group Integrations > Case Mask Configuration 2. Maintenance item: Case Mask Configuration (accession numbering)

    3. Business purpose and scope. A case mask is the pattern of an accession number: a prefix, the year and a running sequence, for example MFT26-0029. Each mask has its own prefix, pattern and counter, and belongs to one scope: the enterprise, a performing-lab facility, or a department. When a case is accessioned, PathScribe looks for a mask in this order: its department, then its performing lab, then the enterprise. A case with no mask anywhere in that chain uses the default pattern O plus a two-digit year, a hyphen and a four-digit sequence. An accession number is permanent and tied to physical tissue and chain of custody, so saving a mask changes the pattern going forward only and never resets the counter.

    4. Prerequisites and dependencies. The Facility and Enterprise scopes read the Facility Dictionary. A department scope reads Departments, which is set up in a later tier. Skip the facility and no facility or enterprise mask can be added; cases then use the default pattern. A scope that already has a mask is not offered again: use Edit.

    # Tier 2: Master Dictionaries and Clinical Foundational Data (Configure Second)

    Tier 2 is the set of lists the laboratory's daily work picks from: departments, specimen types, stains, protocols, containers, cassette colours, physicians, client service levels and the code and classification lists used on reports. None of these lists works alone. A specimen type points at a department, a subspecialty and a protocol. A cassette rule points at a protocol and a colour. A client service level points at a client facility. This is why Tier 2 comes after Tier 1 (the facilities, people and devices in Chapter 2) and has its own order.

    Configure Tier 2 in the order below. Each screen carries a Setup sequence box with the same information, and the builder checks that no screen requires one that comes after it.

    1. Governing Bodies: the standards bodies and their retention figures. ForMedrixAI internal only.
    2. Code Systems: which diagnosis code systems are off, optional or required in each country, and the licences you hold.
    3. Terminology Services: a health check of the code-search services.
    4. Code Import (Bulk): a CSV import of billing codes.
    5. Departments: the coarse classification of a specimen at intake.
    6. Subspecialties: the pathology work groups and their routing.
    7. Diagnostic Catalog: stains, antibodies, molecular tests, sectioning protocols and quick-order macros.
    8. Protocol Dictionary: the processing workflow for a specimen.
    9. Container Types: the containers specimens arrive in.
    10. Specimen Dictionary: the specimen types, tying the lists above together.
    11. Flags: case and specimen flags.
    12. Asset Location Dictionary: named physical locations and mortuary storage slots.
    13. Cold Chain: storage units, condition types and temperature readings.
    14. Specimen Deficiencies: deficiency and resolution types.
    15. Organ maps: colours, patterns and question bindings for the anatomical maps.
    16. Cassette Colors: the colour dictionary.
    17. Cassette Routing Rules: which colour a cassette gets.
    18. Ink Colors: the margin ink colours.
    19. Reagent & Solution Lots: lot, expiry and QC status of reagents.
    20. Physicians: ordering and submitting physicians.
    21. Facility Configuration: client accounts (the same screen as the Facility Dictionary).
    22. Client service levels: turnaround promises per client.
    23. Abnormal Trigger Rules: the field and value pairs that flag a case.
    24. Cytology tab: the landing page for the cytology settings.
    25. Nomenclature System: which reporting system cytology uses.
    26. Interpretation and Recommendations: the cytology category lists.
    27. Non-GYN Classification (Milan/Paris): salivary and urinary categories.
    28. Screening Strategy: co-testing or HPV-first, and recall windows.
    29. Non-GYN Routing: which worklist a non-gynaecological case goes to.
    30. Country and laboratory rules: workload cap, look-back, urgent signature and screening intervals.
    31. Assisted Instrumentation: whole slide imaging or traditional review.
    32. Cyto-Histologic Correlation (SNOMED): the SNOMED severity ranks used in correlation.

    The parts below follow the subject, not the setup order: Part A the anatomic pathology specialties, Part B specimens and tissue, Part C containers, cassettes and ink, Part D stains and protocols, Part E code libraries, and Part F physicians, clients and governing bodies.

    Status words. Each screen shows one of the five status words from the authoring standard: Built, Demonstration, Partial, Planned, Not built. Almost every dictionary in this chapter has a production service and a written API contract, so most are Built. The exceptions are named on the screen: the Organ maps settings and the Code Systems policy are kept in the browser only, and the Cold Chain readings are simulated.

    What every dictionary screen shares. - A change needs the screen's own config:...:manage capability. Without it you can open the screen and see the data, but the controls are greyed out. The capabilities in this chapter are marked high risk, so every check (allowed or refused) is written to the audit log. - Most dictionaries here are held per performing lab or Global (every lab). A name or code must be unique inside one lab, or inside Global. - Most lists do not delete. A row is made Inactive, which keeps every record that already uses it. - A name or code that arrives from an order and matches nothing creates an Unverified row (Departments, Physicians, Asset Locations and Facilities do this). The row works, but someone should check it and select Verify.

    # Part A: Anatomic Pathology Specialties

    Home › Configuration

    This part holds the screens that set up the laboratory's departments and work groups, and the Cytology tab. PathScribe does not have one "specialty" screen. The five anatomic pathology specialties are set up through several screens that are listed here, so the table says for each one what exists and what does not.

    Specialty What you can configure today What does not exist
    Surgical pathology The Surgical Tissue department and its default grossing template; the SURGICAL_TISSUE specimen category on the Specimen Dictionary; organ maps and the protocol and cassette dictionaries in Parts B to D. A separate "surgical pathology" settings screen.
    Cytopathology The Fluid / Cytology department; the GYN_CYTOLOGY and NON_GYN_CYTOLOGY specimen categories; the whole Cytology tab (eight screens in this chapter and four more in Chapters 4 and 8). None. This is the only specialty with its own settings tab.
    Dermatopathology A subspecialty named Dermatopathology (seeded), and a built-in case routing rule that sends skin keywords to it. Mohs micrographic surgery stage maps are part of the organ maps. A dermatopathology department, specimen category or settings screen.
    Hematopathology A subspecialty named Hematopathology (seeded), and a built-in case routing rule that sends haematology keywords to it. A hematopathology department, specimen category or settings screen.
    Autopsy The AUTOPSY specimen category on the Specimen Dictionary; mortuary storage slots and an occupancy view on the Asset Location Dictionary; autopsy sectioning protocols in the Protocol Dictionary; the AUTOPSY workstation group discipline (Workstation Groups); and the AUTOPSY_PAD and AUTOPSY_FAD turnaround target types on the TAT Configuration tab. An autopsy tab or an autopsy-specific maintenance screen.

    The built-in case routing rules that use these subspecialties are on Routing Rules (Chapter 4).

    # Departments

    Home › Configuration › System › Clinical Lookups › Departments

    3. Business purpose and scope. A department is the coarse classification of a specimen at intake: for example Surgical Tissue, Fluid / Cytology, Histology-Only / Consultation. It decides which grossing template a case starts with, whether the department keeps records for a different length of time than the jurisdiction's default, and which laboratory director and accreditation number print in its report header. The Case Mask link on the edit window takes you to Case Mask Configuration, where the department's accession number mask is set.

    4. Prerequisites and dependencies. The retention override is checked against the floor set on Governing Bodies for the current jurisdiction. If no body has a retention figure for the jurisdiction, there is no floor to check against. The list of grossing templates is fixed in the product (three choices), so it does not depend on another screen. Departments are read by the Specimen Dictionary (each specimen type names a department), by the Protocol Dictionary (a new protocol in a fluid department starts as a decant track) and by order intake, which creates an Unverified department when an order names one that does not exist.

    1. Navigation: Configuration tab System > group Clinical Lookups 2. Maintenance item: Subspecialties

    3. Business purpose and scope. A subspecialty is a pathology work group such as GI, Breast, Dermatopathology or Hematopathology. Each one can be a workgroup (cases are assigned to named pathologists) or a pool (any member may claim a case). A subspecialty owns a list of specimen types, a list of pathologists and residents, and a list of facilities. Routing rules send cases to it, and the slide-distribution quick picker lists the active ones. A system-managed pool named General Pathology is the fallback for cases that match nothing else.

    4. Prerequisites and dependencies. The Physicians tab lists staff whose role is Pathologist or Resident, and the Facilities tab lists active facilities. Create both in Tier 1 first (Members, Facility Dictionary), or those tabs are empty. Specimen types can be linked here, or later from the Specimen Dictionary editor, where each specimen type names one subspecialty. A specimen type can belong to only one subspecialty.

    Home › Configuration › System › Lab Materials & Workflows

    # Specimen Dictionary

    Home › Configuration › System › Lab Materials & Workflows › Specimen Dictionary

    Status: Built

    1. Navigation: Configuration tab System > group Lab Materials & Workflows 2. Maintenance item: Specimen Dictionary

    3. Business purpose and scope. The master list of specimen types. Each one names the type, procedure and anatomical site, and carries the department, subspecialty, processing protocol, default stains and a base billing code. The Specimen Category drives worklist routing and accessioning behaviour (surgical, GYN cytology, non-GYN cytology, autopsy, molecular, consult). Order intake matches the specimen text on an order against this list. A match that is not exact raises a deficiency.

    4. Prerequisites and dependencies. The editor picks from three other lists: Department from Departments, Subspecialty from Subspecialties and Processing Protocol from the active protocols in the Protocol Dictionary. Skip any of them and that picklist is empty, so the specimen type is saved without it. The protocol also supplies the cassette type, and Cassette Routing Rules match on the protocol, so a specimen type with no protocol cannot match a rule that names one. Default Stains is plain text and is not checked against the Diagnostic Catalog.

The anatomical maps shown beside a synoptic report (prostate sector and biopsy maps, breast clock face, colorectal polyp, rectal and renal resection, oral cavity, neck dissection, Mohs stages) are always drawn from the answers to the synoptic.     # Part C: Container, Cassette and Slide Type Configurations

    Home › Configuration › System › Lab Materials & Workflows

    This part holds the containers a specimen arrives in, the cassette colours and the rules that choose a colour, and the ink colours used on margins.

    There is no slide type screen. PathScribe has no dictionary of slide types, and no slide type picklist anywhere in Configuration. What it does have is the Slides count on each step of a Protocol Dictionary entry (how many slides a step cuts), the Sectioning Protocols and Quick-Order Macros on the Diagnostic Catalog (levels and serial sections), and the label layout on Label Designer.     # Cassette Routing Rules

    Home › Configuration › System › Lab Materials & Workflows › Cassette Routing Rules

    Status: Built

    1. Navigation: Configuration tab System > group Lab Materials & Workflows 2. Maintenance item: Cassette Routing Rules

    3. Business purpose and scope. Decides which cassette colour a block gets, from the protocol, order priority, origin station, ordering facility and case type. Every condition you set must match. A condition left unset matches anything, so a rule with no conditions is a catch-all. When more than one rule matches, the highest priority weight wins, and the earlier-created rule wins a tie. A rule is ignored outside its Effective From and Effective To dates. The cassette type (format) is never set here: it comes from the matched protocol's processing format.

    4. Prerequisites and dependencies. The protocol picklist reads the Protocol Dictionary, the colour picklist reads Cassette Colors, the origin station picklist reads Scan Stations and the ordering facility picklist reads the Facility Dictionary. Skip the colours and the Cassette Color list is empty, so no rule can be saved.

    # Part D: Processing Protocols, Stains, Antibodies and Special Stains Masters

    Home › Configuration › System

    This part holds the master lists for everything done to a specimen after grossing: the stains, antibodies and molecular tests, the lots of reagent used, and the processing protocols.

    Where antibodies and special stains live. PathScribe has no separate antibody screen and no separate special stain screen. Both are entries on the Diagnostic Catalog (the stain dictionary), told apart by Category: an antibody is an entry with the category IHC (or Immunofluorescence) that carries an Antibody Clone and a Vendor, and a special stain is an entry with the category Special Stain. Lots of antibodies and special stain kits are tracked on Reagent & Solution Lots.

    # Diagnostic Catalog

    Home › Configuration › System › Lab Materials & Workflows › Diagnostic Catalog

    Status: Built

    1. Navigation: Configuration tab System > group Lab Materials & Workflows 2. Maintenance item: Diagnostic Catalog (the stain dictionary). It has four tabs: Diagnostic Assays, Sectioning Protocols, Quick-Order Macros and Master Targets.

    3. Business purpose and scope. One catalog for stains (routine, special, immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, cytology), molecular tests (FISH, PCR, NGS) and other tests. A Diagnostic Assay is the thing ordered. A Sectioning Protocol says how the block is cut (for example Level x 3). The two are separate on purpose. A Quick-Order Macro puts one of each into a single ordering shortcut. Master Targets is the list of probes, genes and mutation regions that molecular tests are built from.

    4. Prerequisites and dependencies. The molecular fields pick performing labs and reference labs from the Facility Dictionary. Reference labs need the Reference Lab role. Billing codes are typed in as the billing code of a Billing Dictionary entry, never as a raw CPT code, and the Billing Dictionary is set up later (Tier 7), so a code typed here is not checked when you save. Skip the catalog and the Protocol Dictionary has no stains to put on a step, and Reagent & Solution Lots has none to attach a lot to.

    # Protocol Dictionary

    Home › Configuration › System › Clinical Lookups › Protocol Dictionary

    Status: Built

    1. Navigation: Configuration tab System > group Clinical Lookups 2. Maintenance item: Protocol Dictionary

    3. Business purpose and scope. A protocol is a standalone, reusable processing workflow. It is not tied to one specimen type: you map it from the Processing Protocol field on the Specimen Dictionary, and editing it here changes every specimen type that uses it. A protocol has one or more tracks (for example Light Microscopy, Immunofluorescence, Electron Microscopy). Each track has a material kind (block or decant), a fixative, a processing format, and ordered steps. A step can cut slides, apply stains or be a hold. A protocol can require triage at the bench, with a checklist.

    4. Prerequisites and dependencies. Steps pick stains from the Diagnostic Catalog. The fixative and processing format picklists read two fixed dictionaries that have no maintenance screen (fifteen fixatives and media, four formats: Standard, Megablock, Frozen Block, Resin Grid). A new protocol takes the default fixative and format, and starts as a decant track when its department is a fluid department (Departments). Skip the catalog and the step stain picker is empty.
